messages.subject: Zero Inflated Beta Regression
parts:
Dear STAN-group,

I am trying to implement in STAN a zero-inflated beta regression following Ospina and Ferrari 2012 (http://arxiv.org/pdf/1103.2372.pdf). I used the equation 2.2 to develop the attached model which surprisingly worked, compiled and gave reasonable estimates on a simulated dataset. However as I am pretty new to STAN and bayesian data analysis in general I would like to get feedbacks from people with higher level of expertise than me.

Sincerely yours,
Lionel

PS: Here is the R code used to generate the simulated data and the model

set.seed(20160427)
dat<-data.frame(x=runif(100,-2,2))
mm<-model.matrix(~x,dat)
coefs<-c(-1,2)
mus<-invlogit(mm%*%coefs)
phi<-3
dat$y<-rbeta(n = 100,shape1 = mus*phi,shape2 = (1-mus)*phi)
#count how many 0s or 1s
length(which(dat$y==0 | dat$y==1))
#STAN models
m_zoib<-stan(file = "STAN/ZOIB_1.stan",data = list(N=nrow(mm),K=ncol(mm),y=dat$y,X=mm))

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Zero Inflated Beta Regression
parts:
That's more like a hurdle model than a zero-inflated one.
You should check out the examples in the manual.

You declare the mixing ratio as

real<lower=0,upper=1> a; //the zero-inflation parameter

but then have

for(i in 1:N){
if(y[i] == 0)
increment_log_prob(a);
else
increment_log_prob((1 - a) * beta_log(y[i],alpha[i],beta[i]));
}

The first line should be increment_log_prob(log(a)) or 1 ~ bernoulli(a).
And the second should be log1m(a) + beta_log(...).

Also, y[i] == 0 is odd for a continuous parameter in (0, 1). Sounds
like a data collection defect, or something you should be modeling with
counts rather than proportions.


Having the alpha and beta vary by data point probably won't work
very well, either. It also leaves the alpha[i] and beta[i] ungrounded
in cases where y[i] == 0.

- Bob

messages.author: 5bea1f4b756d0d58
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Zero Inflated Beta Regression
parts:
Dear Bob,

Thank you very much for your reply.

With this model we aim to link the proportion of leaf area removed through invertebrate herbivory with some parameters like plant biomass. We have quite a lot of sample were we did not record any herbivory damage, therefore we have quite some 0s (8% of the samples). I would somehow feel uneasy if I had to drop that many observations ...

Concerning having alpha and beta (the two parameters for the beta distribution) vary per data point, I thought this was the standard approach in a beta regression (See here: https://github.com/mclark--/Miscellaneous-R-Code/blob/master/ModelFitting/Bayesian/rstanBetaRegression.R).

Finally for the model, I looked up for hurdle model in the reference manual, and would you agree that the following syntax would work:

(y[i] == 0) ~bernoulli(a);
if(y[i] > 0)
 increment_log_prob(log1m(a) + beta_log(alpha[i],beta[i]));


Yours,
Lionel
